newsitem.title: MEXICO: Cuban sugar harvest holding up after hot winter.
newsitem.headline: Cuban sugar harvest holding up after hot winter.

text.p: Cuba's sugar harvest, crucial to world markets because of the country's export potential, is holding up after a hot winter and is expected to be slightly above the previous harvest's 4.45 million tonnes.
Cubazucar vice president Iris Nocedo de Leon told reporters at the F.O. Licht World Sugar and Sweetners' Conference here that the current 1996/97 crop would be "slightly above' the 1995/96 cycle.
But she said early crop predictions from October last year of around 5 million tonnes would probably not be met because of the weather and delays of inputs, such as fertilizers.

"There have been delays in the inputs of the crop and delays because of the weather," she said. "We had a hot winter." She added that hurricane systems also flattened some cane fields in the central and Cienfuegos regions of the island, also bringing a setback for the harvest. "More people are needed to cut it," she added.

But she said Cuba was seeing "better yields in general, probably as a consequence of better fertilization and better care" adding that it was the second year that Cuba had found ways of financing input needs to boost the harvest.
Cuba's crop slumped to 3.3 million tonnes in the 1994/95 cycle and rebounded slightly last year but is still below levels recorded in 1990 of more than 8 million tonnes.
Experts believe Cuba could reap 4.7 or 4.8 million tonnes this harvest.
For the 1997/98 harvest, she said she had no figure to hand but that work was being done to "make a good recovery".
When asked what she thought of an analyst's view that Cuba could aim for a feasible goal of six to 6.5 million tonnes per harvest, she said Cuba had no target in such terms. "But it is possible."
The head of the International Sugar Organisation's economics and statistic divisions put forward the suggestion earlier in the conference.
"We are very flexible, we have to be very pragmatic. We need to recover with a cost efficiency," she said
On the export front, Nocedo de Leon said shipments were ongoing as normal but said she had no figures to hand.
Questioned about the impact of the controversial Helms- Burton law in the United States, she admitted it was making things more difficult to trade Cuban sugar.
"It is delaying things, making things more difficult but not stopping us. We have to look for ways to make sure clients are not damaged by the law," she said. She declined to elaborate.
